cue.topic: Describe a decision you made that changed your life
bullets: when and why you made it
how you made up your mind
and explain how it changed your life

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the decision I made three years ago to quit my secure job at a bank and retrain as a physiotherapist. At the time I was twenty-six and earning a decent salary, but I dreaded Monday mornings and felt stuck in a rut. The turning point came when I badly injured my knee playing football. My physiotherapist, a patient woman called Priya, had me back on my feet in just three months, and I was deeply impressed by how much she loved her work. For weeks I weighed up the pros and cons. Leaving a stable income was a huge leap of faith, especially as my parents were worried I would regret it. I talked it over with Priya and with my older brother, who told me to follow my heart, and in the end I took the plunge and handed in my notice. It wasn't easy. I had to dip into my savings, live in a tiny rented room and study late into the night. Even so, I never doubted my choice. Today I work at a busy sports clinic, and seeing a patient walk without pain is incredibly fulfilling. The decision completely changed my life, because I'm now doing something meaningful rather than simply paying the bills. Looking back, I'm so glad I didn't play it safe, and I'd encourage anyone in a similar position to be brave.

questions.q: Why do some people find it hard to make important decisions?
questions.model: I think fear of failure is the main reason. When the stakes are high, people worry about making the wrong call and being judged by others, so they put things off indefinitely. Having too many options can also be paralysing, because every choice means giving something up. Personally, I believe breaking a big decision into smaller steps makes it far less daunting. It also helps to talk things through with someone you trust.

questions.q: To what extent should people take risks in their careers?
questions.model: To a fair extent, I'd say, provided the risk is calculated. Playing it safe may guarantee a steady income, but it can also leave people stagnating in jobs they have outgrown. Taking a chance on a new field often pays off in the long run, as long as you have a financial cushion to fall back on. However, reckless gambles with no plan are rarely wise. The key is to weigh the potential rewards against what you could realistically lose.

questions.q: Should young people be encouraged to follow their passions or to choose stable careers?
questions.model: Ideally a bit of both. Passion keeps people motivated through tough times, but passion alone rarely pays the rent, so a realistic plan matters. I'd encourage young people to explore their interests while they build marketable skills, so that they have more than one string to their bow. Parents sometimes push their children towards secure professions, which is understandable, yet forcing someone into a career they dislike can lead to burnout. Ultimately, the decision should belong to the individual.

questions.q: What might be the consequences of living in a society that changes so quickly?
questions.model: Rapid change brings both opportunities and strains. On the plus side, new technologies create jobs and make daily life easier. On the downside, older workers may struggle to keep pace, and traditional communities can lose their identity. People may also feel overwhelmed when nothing stays the same for long. I think governments need to cushion the impact by funding retraining schemes and protecting cultural heritage, so that nobody gets left behind.

questions.q: Do you think people today are more or less afraid of change than in the past?
questions.model: Probably less, at least among younger generations. People used to stay in one town and one job for life, whereas today changing careers or moving abroad is almost the norm. Social media also exposes us to different lifestyles, which makes alternatives feel within reach. That said, uncertainty about the economy leaves many people clinging to what they know. So the fear hasn't vanished; it has simply shifted from change itself to the cost of getting it wrong.

questions.q: How far do you agree that making mistakes is essential for personal growth?
questions.model: I agree to a large extent. Mistakes force us to reflect and adapt, and many of my most valuable lessons came from getting things wrong. Successful entrepreneurs often describe early failures as stepping stones rather than disasters. However, some errors, such as medical blunders, carry serious consequences, so the idea doesn't apply everywhere. In everyday life, though, I think learning from experience builds resilience and a healthier attitude to risk over time.
